power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text: We found no codebook or README documentation for the 828 extracted data columns.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 828 data columns across 143 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.
#### Duplicated Column Names

- **Duplicated column names in `scimagojr_2024.csv`.** 1 column name appears more than once (worst: `Publisher`×2), so 2 of the file's 27 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Liver transplantation is often the only lifesaving option for acute liver failure (ALF); however, the predictors of short-term mortality (death within one year) after living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) for ALF have yet to be defined. We retrospectively collected patients â‰¥18 years old who underwent LDLT for ALF between 2010 and 2020 at 35 centers in Asia. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify the clinical variables related to short-term mortality and establish a novel scoring system. The Kaplan-Meier method was performed to explore the association between the score and overall survival. Of the 339 recipients, 46 (13.6%) died within 1 year after LDLT. Multivariate analyses revealed 4 independent risk factors for death: use of vasopressors or mechanical ventilation, the higher model for end-stage liver disease score, and a lower graft-to-recipient weight ratio. The internally validated c-statistic of the short-term mortality after transplant (SMT) score derived from these 4 variables was 0.80 (95% confidence interval: 0.74-0.87). The SMT score successfully stratified recipients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups with 1-year overall survival rates of 96%, 80%, and 50%, respectively. In conclusion, our novel SMT score based on 4 predictors will guide ALF recipient and living donor selection. | Distant metastasis of cancer is a significant contributor to cancer-related complications, and early identification of unidentified stomach adenocarcinoma is crucial for a positive prognosis. Changes inDNA methylation are being increasingly recognized as a crucial factor in predicting cancer progression. Within this research, we developed machine learning and deep learning models for distinguishing distant metastasis in samples of stomach adenocarcinoma based on DNA methylation profile. Employing deep neural networks (DNN), support vector machines (SVM), random forest (RF), Naive Bayes (NB) and decision tree (DT), and models for forecasting distant metastasis in stomach adenocarcinoma. The results show that the performance of DNN is better than that of other models, AUC and AUPR achieving 99.9Â % and 99.5Â % respectively. Additionally, a weighted random sampling technique was utilized to address the issue of imbalanced datasets, enabling the identification of crucial methylation markers associated with functionally significant genes in stomach distant metastasis tumors with greater performance. | (1) Background: Arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is the preferred type of vascular access for dialysis in patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). However, the primary patency of AVF at one year is under 70% due to several risk factors and comorbidities. Leukocyte glucose index (LGI), a new biomarker based on blood leukocytes and glucose values, has been found to be associated with poor outcomes in cardiovascular disease. The aim of this study is to analyze the impact of LGI on the long-term primary patency of AVF following dialysis initiation. (2) Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study in which we initially enrolled 158 patients with ESKD admitted to the Vascular Surgery Department of the Emergency County Hospital of Targu Mures, Romania, to surgically create an AVF for dialysis between January 2020 and July 2023. The primary endpoint was AVF failure, defined as the impossibility of performing a chronic dialysis session due to severe restenosis or AVF thrombosis. After follow-up, we categorized patients into two groups based on their AVF status: ""functional AVF"" for those with a permeable AVF and ""AVF failure"" for those with vascular access dysfunction. (3) Results: Patients with AVF failure had a higher prevalence of atrial fibrillation (p = 0.013) and diabetes (p = 0.028), as well as a higher LGI value (1.12 vs. 0.79, p < 0.001). At ROC analysis, LGI had the strongest association with the outcome, with an AUC of 0.729, and an optimal cut-off value of 0.95 (72.4% sensitivity and 68% specificity). In Kaplan-Meier survival analyses, patients in the highest tertile (T3) of LGI had a significantly higher incidence of AVF failure compared to those in tertile 1 (p = 0.019). Moreover, we found that patients with higher baseline LGI values had a significantly higher risk of AVF failure during follow-up (HR: 1.48, p = 0.003). The association is independent of age and sex (HR: 1.65, p = 0.001), cardiovascular risk factors (HR: 1.63, p = 0.012), and pre-operative vascular mapping determinations (HR: 3.49, p = 0.037). (4) Conclusions: In conclusion, high preoperative values of LGI are positively associated with long-term AVF failure. The prognostic role of the biomarker was independent of age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, and pre-operative vascular mapping determinations. | Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is an autoimmune disease that involves inflammation of blood vessels. There is increasing evidence that platelets play a crucial role not only in hemostasis but also in inflammation and innate immunity. In this study, we explored the relationship between platelet count, clinical characteristics, and the prognosis of patients with AAV. We divided 187 patients into two groups based on their platelet count. Clinicopathological data and prognostic information were retrospectively gathered from medical records. Univariate and multivariate regression analyses were used to identify risk factors for prognosis, including end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and mortality. The cutoff point for platelet count was set at 264.5â€‰Ã—â€‰109/L, as determined by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for predicting progression to ESRD in patients with AAV. We observed patients with low platelet count (plateletsâ€‰<â€‰264.5â€‰Ã—â€‰109/L) had lower leukocytes, hemoglobin, complement, acute reactants, and worse renal function (P for eGFRâ€‰<â€‰0.001). They were also more likely to progress to ESRD or death compared to the high platelet count group (plateletsâ€‰>â€‰264.5â€‰Ã—â€‰109/L) (Pâ€‰<â€‰0.0001, Pâ€‰=â€‰0.0338, respectively). Low platelet count was potentially an independent predictor of poor renal prognosis in the multivariate regression analysis [HR 1.670 (95% CI 1.019-2.515), Pâ€‰=â€‰0.014]. Lower platelet count at diagnosis is associated with more severe clinical characteristics and impaired renal function. Therefore, platelet count may be an accessible prognostic indicator for renal outcomes in patients with AAV. | Soluble P-selectin (sP-selectin) has been proposed as a potential biomarker for venous thromboembolism (VTE) diagnosis with interesting results. However, its role in predicting early mortality in pulmonary embolism (PE) remains unexplored. This observational, prospective, single-center study enrolled consecutive patients aged 18 or older with confirmed acute symptomatic PE and no prior anticoagulation. The study aims to assess the prognostic capacity of sP-selectin measured at the time of PE diagnosis for short-term mortality and major bleeding. A total of 196 patients, with a mean age of 69.1â€‰years (SD 17), were included, of whom 52.6% were male. Within 30â€‰days, 9.7% of patients (nâ€‰=â€‰19) died, and 5.1% (nâ€‰=â€‰10) suffered major bleeding. PE risk stratification revealed 4.6% (nâ€‰=â€‰9) with high-risk PE, 34.7% (nâ€‰=â€‰68) with intermediate-high-risk PE, 38.3% (nâ€‰=â€‰75) with intermediate-low-risk PE, and 22.5% (nâ€‰=â€‰44) with low-risk PE according to the European Society of Cardiology score. Mean plasma sP-selectin levels were comparable between survivors and non-survivors (489.7â€‰ng/mL Â±63 vs. 497.3â€‰ng/mL Â±51; pâ€‰=â€‰.9). The ROC curve for 30-day all-cause mortality and major bleeding yielded an AUC of 0.49 (95% CI 0.36-0.63) and 0.46 (95% CI 0.24-0.68), respectively. Multivariate and survival analyses were precluded due to lack of significance. sP-selectin was not useful for predicting short-term mortality or major bleeding in patients with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism. Further studies are required to clarify the role of sP-selectin in VTE, particularly in prognosticating PE outcomes.

It may serve as a new method for comprehensive detection and diagnosis of salivary gland injury. | This study aims to identify biomarkers for reliably predicting diabetic kidney disease (DKD), systematically characterize serum metabolites and gut microbiota in DKD patients, and investigate the correlation between differential serum metabolites and gut microbiota. Differential metabolites were identified through univariate (t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test, P < 0.05) and multivariate analyses (OPLS-DA model, VIP > 1, P < 0.05), followed by selection using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO). In the DKD group compared to the DM and NC groups, 39 and 60 differential serum metabolites were identified, respectively (VIP > 1, P < 0.01). Among these, 36 serum metabolites, including alpha-Hydroxyisobutyric acid, were significantly elevated in DKD patients compared to those with DM. Of these, 28 metabolites showed a negative correlation with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), while 29 showed a positive correlation with urine albumin creatinine ratio (UACR). Patients with DKD were further categorized into subgroups (DKD middle and DKD early) based on eGFR (eGFR < 90 ml/min/1.73m2, eGFR ≥ 90 ml/min/1.73m2), revealing 23 differential metabolites. Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota was evident in DKD patients, with lower relative abundances of g_Prevotella and g_Faecalibacterium compared to the DM and NC groups. Subgroup analysis indicated decreased relative abundances of g_Prevotella and g_Faecalibacterium in the DKD middle group, along with a decrease in g_Klebsiella compared to the DKD early group, which correlated positively with DKD patients' eGFR. There were 11 common metabolites among the three groups of differential metabolites. Among these, three serum metabolites-imidazolepropionic acid, adipoylcarnitine, and 1-methylhistidine-were identified as predictive serum metabolic markers. Disease prediction models (logistic regression models) were constructed based on these three metabolites combined with three genera of bacteria. These models demonstrated strong discriminatory power for diagnosing patients with DKD compared to patients with DM (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) = 0.939 and precision-recall curve (AUPR) = 0.940). The models also effectively discriminated between patients with DKD and NCs (0.976, 0.973). This study revealed distinctive serum metabolites and gut microbiota in patients with DKD. It demonstrated the potential utility of three specific serum metabolites and three genera of bacteria in diagnosing patients with DKD and assessing their renal dysfunction.

Physio-cognitive decline syndrome (PCDS) is a reversible condition affecting physical and cognitive health in older adults. Early detection is essential to facilitate timely interventions. This study aimed to evaluate wrist rotation metrics as potential biomarkers for PCDS and explore their applicability in digital health tools. This pilot study recruited 50 community-dwelling individuals aged 50 years or older from Yi-Lan County, Taiwan, including 19 with PCDS and 31 robust participants. Wrist rotation movements were assessed using a custom device, and statistical analyses, including logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, were performed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the metrics. Two rotation metrics, Rotate (60°-30°) and the ratio Rotate (30°-90°)/Rotate (60°-90°), were significantly associated with PCDS. The ratio metric demonstrated high sensitivity, making it suitable for initial screening, while Rotate (60°-30°) exhibited high specificity, supporting its use as a confirmatory test. These complementary roles highlight the potential of these metrics in tiered diagnostic frameworks. Wrist rotation metrics show promise as scalable and non-invasive tools for detecting PCDS. These findings support their integration into digital platforms, such as smartphone applications, for early screening and intervention. Further studies are needed to validate these findings in larger, diverse populations and to assess their utility in monitoring disease progression and guiding interventions to improve physical and cognitive health. | Forest fires are a significant global environmental hazard, causing widespread economic losses and ecological damage to natural habitats. Biodiversity-rich regions like Mizoram, a northeastern Indian state known for its lush forests and a part of Indo-Burma Biodiversity Hotspot, are particularly vulnerable to these fires. Between 2012 and 2021, Mizoram incurred losses amounting to approximately $8,910,000 USD due to wildfires. This study addresses the urgent need for high-resolution forest fire susceptibility mapping for southern Mizoram (Lunglei, Lawngtlai, Serchhip, and Tlabung), highlighting the region's ecological fragility and vulnerability. We employed six machine learning (ML) algorithms-AdaBoost, Decision Tree, Gaussian Process, K-Nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine and analyzed ten wildfire conditioning factors. These factors include topographical elements (DEM, slope, aspect, curvature, TWI), vegetation indices (pre-fire EVI, pre-fire VARI), anthropogenic factors (LULC), and solar radiation. A forest fire inventory was created using high-resolution satellite images from April 2021 through visual manual interpretation. Feature importance analysis using Gini Impurity revealed that pre-fire NDMI, EVI, DEM, aspect, and solar radiation were the most significant contributors. Performance metrics such as average accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the curve (AUC), and G-mean were used to evaluate the ML algorithms. AUC values ranged from 0.84 to 0.91, with accuracy scores between 0.74 and 0.81. Among the models, the Random Forest algorithm demonstrated the best performance across all metrics. Lawngtlai exhibited the highest susceptibility (64%, 869.66 km2), followed by Tlabung (38%, 956.09 km2), Lunglei (27%, 556.57 km2), and Serchhip (21%, 21.72 km2). Overall, 37.01% (2677.21 km2) of the study area was classified as highly susceptible. Our analysis further indicates that lower elevations and specific aspect orientations-namely East, Southeast, Southwest, and South-substantially influence forest fire susceptibility. Finally, the forest fire susceptibility map was validated using high-resolution Planet images. This study demonstrates that ML-based susceptibility estimation can be used to implement effective natural resource management and proactive measures to mitigate the environmental impact of forest fires. | Laryngeal cancer (LCA) is a prevalent head and neck malignancy. However, laryngoscopic image interpretation remains experience-dependent, resulting in diagnostic variability, particularly in resource-limited settings. This study aimed to develop a deep learning model to enhance lesion detection, guide biopsies, and streamline diagnostic processes. Retrospective study of a classification network. Five medical centers in China. A dataset comprising 16,587 laryngoscopic images from 2585 patients representing 10 distinct laryngeal lesions was established. First, TransCL was developed and validated on multiple independent test sets in comparison with existing models. Second, the model was evaluated on unseen lesion types to assess its generalizability. Third, its ability to predict malignant transformation in benign lesions was assessed against expert annotations. Finally, TransCL predictions were compared with diagnoses made by laryngologists. TransCL demonstrated outstanding performance across all test sets, achieving an area under the curve of 0.978 (0.974-0.982), accuracy of 0.942 (0.938-0.945), F1-score of 0.961 (0.959-0.963), and Matthews Correlation Coefficient of 0.843 (0.831-0.855) in the internal validation. Performance remained robust in external validations, outperforming existing models. The model demonstrated strong generalization to unseen lesion types and reliably predicted malignant transformation risk in benign lesions. Compared with human experts, TransCL outperformed junior laryngologists and several senior laryngologists, achieving performance achieving performance comparable to that of top senior laryngologists. TransCL demonstrated high robustness, accuracy, and generalizability, with diagnostic performance comparable to that of experienced clinicians in LCA detection and lesion risk assessment, suggesting its potential for clinical applications. | Glioma is characterized by a poor prognosis and limited possibilities for treatment. Previous studies have developed prediction models for glioma using genetic, clinical, pathological, imaging and other aspects; however, few studies have combined these data. The current study is intended to fully utilize medical data from the routine practice of glioma care and develop a model with the assistance of machine learning. Multiple factors-including demographic features, radiomic features, laboratory biomarkers, and pathological features-were collected from two Class Three hospitals in China. Preoperative images and blood tests were quantified with machine learning methods. The survival time was documented during follow-up. Multivariate Cox regression and seven machine learning algorithms were used for modeling. A total of 674 glioma patients from two centers were enrolled. Fifteen radiomic features (RFs) and ten laboratory biomarkers were used to create the RF score and blood score. A clinicopathological-radiomic-blood model (CRBM) was created to stratify the mortality risk of glioma patients (P < 0.0001). The AUC of the Cox-based model was 0.913 (0.886-0.940) on the training dataset and 0.802 (0.738-0.865) on the validation dataset, and the AUCs of the XGBoost model on the same datasets were 0.954 (0.935-0.973) and 0.761 (0.693-0.829), respectively. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method suggested the contribution of preoperative imaging and laboratory data to the model. The CRBM is able to predict the survival of glioma patients with acceptable accuracy. Our work suggests the considerable potential of combined clinically derived data in predicting glioma survival and the utility of machine learning in variable selection and model construction. | Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a leading cause of trauma-related mortality within 30 days in severe trauma patients. Current diagnostic methods have limitations, leading to an urgent need to identify early diagnostic biomarkers of VTE. To screen early diagnostic biomarkers of VTE following severe trauma by integrating metabolomics and proteomics. The existing plasma metabolomics and proteomics data from 72 severe trauma patients with (22 cases) and without (49 cases) VTE were retrospectively analyzed. By comparing two groups, early diagnostic biomarkers of VTE in severe trauma patients were identified. 210 differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) and 11 DEPs (DEPs) were identified. We screened the top 10 DEMs and 11 DEPs as early diagnostic biomarkers for VTE after severe trauma, then developed two panels using top 10 DEMs (AUC=0.952) and 11 DEPs (AUC=0.955), respectively. By integrating metabolomics and proteomics, we developed a diagnostic panel consisting of LPC16:0 and FA7, which demonstrated superior diagnostic efficacy (AUC = 0.937). This study identified potential biomarkers of VTE after severe trauma, providing a novel strategy for early precision diagnosis, providing new insights into the pathogenesis of VTE after severe trauma, and establishing a translational framework for developing early diagnostic biomarker panels.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 828 columns across 143 data files.
#### Issues Identified

140 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 143 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report:
This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 24 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:24, File = c("01_scimago_journal_ranking_extraction.R", 
"01_simulate_roc_curves.R", "02_article_extraction.R", "02_article_extraction_2.R", 
"02_extract_auc_roc.R", "03_pilot_articles.R", "03_protocol_flowcharts.R", 
"04_rayyan_included.R", "05_analysis_pilot.R", "05_predict_research_time.R",

"07_screening_assessment.R", "07_screening_assessment_2.R", "08_data_code_availability.R", 
"09_claude_validate.R", "09_second_extract.R", "10_analysis_adrian.R",

"—", "01_scimago_journal_ranking_extraction.R", "01_scimago_journal_ranking_extraction.R, 02_article_extraction.R", 
"01_simulate_roc_curves.R", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "07_screening_assessment.R", "—",

"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "numeric"
)), row.names = c(NA, -24L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
**3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `02_data/journal_rank.rdata` to `02_data/journal_rank.Rdata` (in 03_pilot_articles.R); `02_data/q_one_journals.rdata` to `02_data/q_one_journals.Rdata` (in 02_article_extraction.R); `02_data/q_one_journals.rdata` to `02_data/q_one_journals.Rdata` (in 02_article_extraction_2.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
**3 file names in the code are not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("03_pilot_articles.R", "02_article_extraction.R", 
"02_article_extraction_2.R"), "Name in the code" = c("journal_rank.rdata", 
"q_one_journals.rdata", "q_one_journals.rdata"), "Name in the deposit" = c("journal_rank.Rdata", 
"q_one_journals.Rdata", "q_one_journals.Rdata")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `example_data.csv`.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 24 scripts: 14 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **4 scripts need the internet**, which is off during the run: 02_article_extraction.R, 02_article_extraction_2.R, 03_pilot_articles.R, 05_predict_research_time.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `10_plots_for_slides.R` after `10_analysis.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first; a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

**Dependency-unavailable errors**
**3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

text.text: Background Previous research has shown that clinical prediction models have likely been "hacked" to meet arbitrary performance thresholds.
However, this work only assessed abstracts, could not identify models with a perfect AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of 1, and did not examine other performance metrics.
Methods We collected data from full texts and validated a large language model to extract data from a random sample of Q1 journal articles for 2025.

We examined if hacking occurred in the AUC value, sensitivity and specificity, and checked if articles correctly reported the AUC value from corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves.
Results We identified 2,001 prediction model articles that reported 15,656 AUC values.

We found a striking excess of results near perfect prediction and at multiples of five and ten for the AUC, sensitivity and specificity, indicating likely manipulated data, methods or publication bias.
Around 1 in 40 AUC values were reported outside of their confidence intervals, and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match their reported AUC value.
Conclusion We have shown that not only the AUC value, but the sensitivity and specificity are being hacked, likely to help the authors publish their paper at the cost of evidence for practice.
Excess models that are not representative of their true performance may misguide clinicians, distort the literature, and make it harder to find prediction models that are useful for practice.
Clinical prediction is a rapidly growing field of research, with nearly 250,000 new models published between 1950 and 2024 (1).
text.formatted: Clinical prediction is a rapidly growing field of research, with nearly 250,000 new models published between 1950 and 2024 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Extensive problems exist in current publications, including poor reporting, and inappropriate data or methods leading to many wasteful studies (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) (7) (8).
text.formatted: Extensive problems exist in current publications, including poor reporting, and inappropriate data or methods leading to many wasteful studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: As stark examples of poor practice, a statistician-led review found only 7 of 606 published COVID-19 prognostic models were of sufficient quality for clinical practice, while a sepsis model used in hundreds of United States Hospitals missed two-thirds of patients with sepsis (9, 10).
text.formatted: As stark examples of poor practice, a statistician-led review found only 7 of 606 published COVID-19 prognostic models were of sufficient quality for clinical practice, while a sepsis model used in hundreds of United States Hospitals missed two-thirds of patients with sepsis <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: These issues contribute to research waste and misguided predictions which can lead patients to receiving incorrect treatments or not receiving necessary treatments.
The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) value, is a widely used metric of a model's ability to discriminate between events (e.g., death versus survival).
The AUC value ranges from 0.5 (a coin toss) to 1.0 (perfect discrimination).
Arbitrary thresholds have been purported at 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9, providing incentives for researchers to target these thresholds (4, 11).
text.formatted: Arbitrary thresholds have been purported at 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9, providing incentives for researchers to target these thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>.

text.text: This incentive may tempt researchers to potentially 'hack' their data, methods or reporting to inflate these values for their models (12).
text.formatted: This incentive may tempt researchers to potentially 'hack' their data, methods or reporting to inflate these values for their models <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: The appropriate design and reporting of models is necessary for transparency and implementation into practice, with various expert-led guidelines being published (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: The appropriate design and reporting of models is necessary for transparency and implementation into practice, with various expert-led guidelines being published <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Unfortunately, there is little evidence these guidelines have been widely implemented (16).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, there is little evidence these guidelines have been widely implemented <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Recently, researchers examined the distributions of AUC values, finding evidence of potentially inflated model performances (4).
text.formatted: Recently, researchers examined the distributions of AUC values, finding evidence of potentially inflated model performances <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: They were shown to have excess results around arbitrary thresholds, indicating potential publication bias and researchers inflating model performancestermed AUC-hacking (4).
However, the study only assessed values reported in abstracts where researchers may report the best performing models, and the study could not assess models with an AUC of 1.0.

Additionally, no other performance metrics were examined, nor was it checked if the AUC values were correctly reported against the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve Publish or perish culture has spurred questionable research practices in psychology, ecological and evolutionary research, and biomedical research (17) (18) (19).
text.formatted: Additionally, no other performance metrics were examined, nor was it checked if the AUC values were correctly reported against the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve Publish or perish culture has spurred questionable research practices in psychology, ecological and evolutionary research, and biomedical research <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: If these practices are also widespread in prediction model research published in high ranking journals it is likely to be consequential to outcomes as these journals generally receive more readers and are therefore more likely to influence practice (20, 21).
text.formatted: If these practices are also widespread in prediction model research published in high ranking journals it is likely to be consequential to outcomes as these journals generally receive more readers and are therefore more likely to influence practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: As previous research has shown, model development studies produce larger AUC values than those in subsequent validation studies (22) (23) (24) (25) (26), indicating there may be substantial and clinically meaningful differences between a model's numeric and clinical performance.
text.formatted: As previous research has shown, model development studies produce larger AUC values than those in subsequent validation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref>, indicating there may be substantial and clinically meaningful differences between a model's numeric and clinical performance.

text.text: This study aimed to examine if hacking practices exist in recently published clinical prediction models from Q1 journals.
Our primary aim was to check for AUC-hacking in recently published journal article full texts.
We also examined if reported AUC values corresponded with AUC values of the ROC curve, and if there is evidence that sensitivity and specificity values are also hacked.
We assembled a representative sample of recently published clinical prediction model articles.
Journal rankings were downloaded from Scimago (https://www.scimagojr.com/journalrank.php) for 2024 on January 13, 2026.
text.formatted: Journal rankings were downloaded from Scimago (<ref type="url" target="https://www.scimagojr.com/journalrank.php">https://www.scimagojr.com/journalrank.php</ref>) for 2024 on January 13, 2026.

text.text: Results were filtered to Q1 ranked journals.
The PubMed ID, title and abstract text were extracted from PubMed using the rentrez package (27) in R (version 4.6.1).
text.formatted: The PubMed ID, title and abstract text were extracted from PubMed using the rentrez package <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref> in R (version 4.6.1).

text.text: The search date was January 13, 2026.
The search returned 63,954 articles.
Our protocol and analysis plan were registered on Feb 5, 2026 (28).
text.formatted: Our protocol and analysis plan were registered on <ref type="bibr">Feb 5, 2026 (28)</ref>.

text.text: This study didn't require ethics approval as it used publicly available data and there are no risks to data collection.
We used a custom filter to gather a representative sample of discrimination performance values from published prediction models.
The AUC value and its commonly substituted terms were searched in the title and abstracts of published articles in PubMed (Supplementary 1).
Articles were included if they were, published in a quartile one journal, had at least one clinical prediction model, and were published in 2025.

Articles were excluded if they were: pharmacokinetic studies which frequently mention "Area under curve" (AUC), meta-analyses, systematic reviews, pooled analyses or tutorial articles; the full text was not accessible; the article was not in English; or was an animal study.
Article screening for eligibility was completed independently, in duplicate, by AG and DB using the software Rayyan (29).
text.formatted: Article screening for eligibility was completed independently, in duplicate, by AG and DB using the software Rayyan <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(29)</ref>.

text.text: Agreement was measured using Gwet's AC1 agreement statistic (30).
text.formatted: Agreement was measured using Gwet's AC1 agreement statistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(30)</ref>.

text.text: First, 10% of the articles were manually screened by both authors.
Discrepancies were discussed between the two reviewers for inclusion or exclusion.
Gwet's AC1 statistic was > 0.8, so, as defined in our protocol (31), AG screened the remaining articles after discussions, to reduce overall screening time. (31).
text.formatted: Gwet's AC1 statistic was > 0.8, so, as defined in our protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(31)</ref>, AG screened the remaining articles after discussions, to reduce overall screening time. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Data from 176 articles were extracted manually and compared to an extraction by a large language model (LLM; Claude Sonnet 4.6) (see Supplementary 2 for LLM prompt).
LLMs have previously shown accurate performance for extracting data from published papers (32).
text.formatted: LLMs have previously shown accurate performance for extracting data from published papers <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(32)</ref>.

text.text: Both the LLM and manual extractions collected the same set of information from the full texts.
Data extracted from full texts were: the AUC, sensitivity and specificity values including confidence intervals, sample size, and number of AUC values.
We also recorded if the model was diagnostic or prognostic, using a developmental or validation study, and if there was an ROC curve.
We validated the LLM by manually extracting data from 176 (9%) articles.
We checked accuracy in extraction by examining 50 values that differed between the manual and the LLM extraction.
These included 50 values where the manual extraction retrieved a value, but the LLM didn't, and 50 values where the LLM extraction retrieved a value, but manual extraction didn't.
We primarily examined if any data were incorrectly extracted.

Reported AUC values were visualised using a histogram with bin widths of 0.01 on a scale of 0.5 to 1.0 while sensitivity and specificity were visualised with bin widths 1 percent on a scale from 0% to 100%.
For example, a bin width of (0.78, 0.79] included values > 0.78 and values ≤ 0.79.
text.formatted: For example, a bin width of (0.78, 0.79] included values > 0.78 and values ≤ 0.79.

text.text: Three smooth estimates of the underlying distribution were fit for the AUC, using a b-spline basis with two to four degrees of freedom.
Each of the models were fit with a random intercept to adjust for repeated values from the same article and used a negative binomial distribution. (4, 33).
text.formatted: Each of the models were fit with a random intercept to adjust for repeated values from the same article and used a negative binomial distribution. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">33)</ref>.

text.text: The best fitting degrees of freedom was assessed by the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and was used to calculate the residuals.
These residuals were visualised in separate histograms.
Alternative models varying the b-spline boundary knots beyond the AUC value limits were used to reduce any fitting artifacts at an AUC of 1 (4,33).
Data from available ROC curves were extracted via a semi-automated process using the PlotDigitizer software (version 3.3.9 Pro).
The PlotDigitizer software has been previously validated as a reliable tool for data extraction (34).
text.formatted: The PlotDigitizer software has been previously validated as a reliable tool for data extraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(34)</ref>.

text.text: We cross-checked the reported in-text AUC value against the AUC value extracted from the ROC curve.
The AUC value was calculated using a trapezoidal function from the extracted coordinates of the ROC curve in the R package bayestest (35).
text.formatted: The AUC value was calculated using a trapezoidal function from the extracted coordinates of the ROC curve in the R package bayestest <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(35)</ref>.

text.text: Differences between reported AUC values and their corresponding value extracted from ROC curves were plotted using a histogram.
Bin widths for the histogram were 0.005.
We examined the number of articles with differences between the reported and extracted AUC value of ≥ 0.02 which would provide evidence of altered reporting.
A symmetric distribution centred on zero would indicate no overall bias.
A skewed positive bimodal distribution would indicate researchers are altering the AUC value in their reporting and was our primary indicator of AUChacking by reporting.
All analyses were undertaken in R (version 4.6.1).
All data and code are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/alexdgibson/cpm_auc) (36).
text.formatted: All data and code are publicly available on GitHub (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/alexdgibson/cpm_auc">https://github.com/alexdgibson/cpm_auc</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(36)</ref>.

text.text: Screening agreement between the two reviewers for the first 220 articles was 0.83 (95% CI = 0.68 to 0.84).
The remaining articles were screened by one reviewer, as this met our a priori agreement criteria above 0.8 (28).
text.formatted: The remaining articles were screened by one reviewer, as this met our a priori agreement criteria above 0.8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: There were 672 additional articles included (34%) that met the inclusion criteria that were inadvertently missed during initial filtering for journal articles.
These . articles were not examined in the ROC curve extractions or validation checks but were reported for all other statistics.
After screening, there were 2,166 out of 3,996 articles remaining.
One-hundred and seventy articles were excluded during full text data collection because they did not contain the required information or were not clinical prediction modelling studies.
There were 2,001 articles included for analysis.

From these 2,001 articles, there was a total of 15,656 AUC values extracted, 7,600 sensitivity values from 1,213 of the 2,001 (61%) articles, and 7,176 specificity values from 1,161 of the 2,001 (58%) articles.
Confidence intervals were reported for 9,002 of the 15,656 AUC values (58%) in 1,329 of the 2,001 articles (66%).
There were 227 AUC values that were outside the associated confidence interval (2.5%) or around 1 in 40.
The mean (SD) sensitivity value was 74 (SD = 19) and the mean specificity value was 77 (SD = 17).
The median number of AUC values per article was 5 (1 st to 3 rd quartile = 3 to 10).
No AUC values below 0.0 were reported, but there was one AUC value erroneously reported above 1.0.
There were large excess results at (0.99,1.0] for the AUC value and (99,100] for sensitivity and specificity values (Figure 2, 3 and 4).
text.formatted: There were large excess results at (0.99,1.0] for the AUC value and (99,100] for sensitivity and specificity values (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>, 3 and 4).

text.text: A large underrepresentation of values at (0.90, 0.99] were seen for the AUC value and (90, 100] for both the sensitivity and specificity values.
Excess results were present across all metrics at or just after multiples of five and ten.
Clear examples of thresholding were seen in the sensitivity value at 50, 60, 70, 75 and 80 (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Clear examples of thresholding were seen in the sensitivity value at 50, 60, 70, 75 and 80 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: While the specificity had larger excess results at 80 and 90 (Figure 4).
text.formatted: While the specificity had larger excess results at 80 and 90 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: We assumed where both the manual and LLM extractions had the same data, it was correctly extracted.
Both methods of extraction contained a similar number of missed or incorrect values.
We were comfortable with these results and expect that a purely manual extraction would give similar results to our LLM-based results (more validation information is in Supplementary 3).
From 200 ROC curves, 189 (95%) AUC values were able to be calculated while 11 (5%) of the ROC curves overlapped with other curves or the figure quality was too poor for accurate extraction.

There was no evidence that researchers were systematically altering the reported AUC value compared to the ROC curve data with a mean (SD) difference between the AUC and ROC of 0.0017 (SD = 0.029) (Figure 5).
text.formatted: There was no evidence that researchers were systematically altering the reported AUC value compared to the ROC curve data with a mean (SD) difference between the AUC and ROC of 0.0017 (SD = 0.029) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>).

text.text: Twelve AUC values differed by less than -0.02 and 14 AUC values differed by more than 0.02 or roughly 1 in 8 ROC curves differed between the AUC value reported in-text and visualised in the ROC curve.
Extreme differences in reported AUC values and derived AUC values were seen with the biggest differences of +0.19 and -0.15 which are likely to be clinically important differences.
Our results support previous research that performative AUC values are likely being targeted in published clinical prediction model research identified by excess results at arbitrary thresholds.
We also found that the sensitivity and specificity are being targeted based on observed excesses at the same thresholds.
We are concerned that metrics are being prioritised by researchers for publication at the cost of accuracy.
Some of these results could be explained by researchers removing outliers or hard to predict patient subgroups, selectively reporting models that overfit the data.
The excess results could also partially be explained by publication bias if these models at purported thresholds are preferentially published.
However, we find this less suggestive from the data as the sensitivity and specificity additionally show evidence of being targeted and these excess results all occur across multiple thresholds.

This is further supported by a symmetric distribution of reporting errors for AUC values against their corresponding ROC curves (Figure 5), and no evidence was present that researchers are actively increasing AUC values in-text.
text.formatted: This is further supported by a symmetric distribution of reporting errors for AUC values against their corresponding ROC curves (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>), and no evidence was present that researchers are actively increasing AUC values in-text.

text.text: These excess results combined with an underrepresentation of expected values between 0.90 and 0.99 show these models close to perfect prediction may have been hacked towards 1.00.
Small sample sizes are a common problem and could cause models to overfit and may explain some of these excess models (37) (38) (39) (40).
text.formatted: Small sample sizes are a common problem and could cause models to overfit and may explain some of these excess models <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(37)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(38)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(39)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(40)</ref>.

text.text: The large excess results at (99,100] for the sensitivity and specificity could, however, be explained by rule-in or rule-out models that are designed to be highly selective for sensitivity or specificity but not the other.

We find the results near 1.0 for AUC values concerning as these higher performing models may be the ones that make their way to practice as they are perceived to be the most accurate and provide a misleading evidence base for clinicians.
These models may be contributing to a medical mirage, appearing numerically excellent on paper but performing less well in practice and misguiding clinical decisions if implemented.
We found that poor reporting practices still persist, despite more than a decade of the TRIPOD+AI reporting guidelines for clinical prediction model research (13).
text.formatted: We found that poor reporting practices still persist, despite more than a decade of the TRIPOD+AI reporting guidelines for clinical prediction model research <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: From our analyses we are unable to determine why incorrect reporting continues, but we speculate researchers are developing numerous models and misreporting them potentially via poor version control.
The median number of AUC values per article was 5 (1 st and 3 rd quartile = 3 to 10) which would support this idea of many models.
Poor reporting practices may also be diluting the literature of models that have real abilities to improve care and decisions.

This situation may reduce the visibility of genuine, high-quality models that may not perform as well but are still clinically useful for their intended use setting (41) Accurate reporting and representation of clinical prediction models is critical for clinicians to understand expected patient outcomes.
text.formatted: This situation may reduce the visibility of genuine, high-quality models that may not perform as well but are still clinically useful for their intended use setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(41)</ref> Accurate reporting and representation of clinical prediction models is critical for clinicians to understand expected patient outcomes.

text.text: We found one model with an AUC value from the ROC curve that was 0.19 worse than the in-text reported value, and another model with an AUC value 0.15 better than the in-text reported value.
Potentially serious and substantial consequences could occur if a model with incorrectly reported performance were used to inform policy or care.

As 1 in 8 models differed in their underlying data and reporting, and model performances reduce when validated or implemented, there is a serious misrepresentation of research occurring in prediction models.
Clinical prediction models are used in practice, influence clinical decisions and thus patient care and outcomes (42, 43).
text.formatted: Clinical prediction models are used in practice, influence clinical decisions and thus patient care and outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">43)</ref>.

text.text: However, clinical guidelines rarely have guidance for appraisal and implementation of prediction models (44), making it plausible for adverse outcomes if these hacked models make their way to practice.
text.formatted: However, clinical guidelines rarely have guidance for appraisal and implementation of prediction models <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(44)</ref>, making it plausible for adverse outcomes if these hacked models make their way to practice.

text.text: Overall, our results indicate 1 in 8 models have AUC values ≥ 0.02 or ≤ 0.02 than in-text reported performances.
Differences between reported and underlying performances will misguide clinicians and, if acted upon, potentially lead to harming patients.
Combined with excess results near perfect prediction and knowing developmental models typically perform better on paper than in validation studies, results in practice could be substantially worse.
We are concerned that prediction models will be making their way into practice which may contribute to worse outcomes for patients.
Journals should not recommend but mandate future prediction model development, validation and impact assessments be reported in full against the TRIPOD+AI guidelines unless justified otherwise.
While policy makers should prioritise real world evidence from patient outcome assessments to direct the use of prediction models in practice (44).
Both the manual extraction and LLM extraction made errors and missed valid data.
As with previous research on LLM use for data extraction, many of these errors by both extraction methods arose from poor reporting of results (32).
text.formatted: As with previous research on LLM use for data extraction, many of these errors by both extraction methods arose from poor reporting of results <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(32)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the AUC value was able to be collected with few errors for both manual and LLM extraction, yet large errors were seen in both manual and LLM extraction for sample size.
Sample size errors were seen when reported as multiple sub-samples of the entire sample, differing splits for development and validation, or many subsamples during inclusion and exclusion decisions.
This extraction failure is not surprising, as clinical prediction models are poorly reported (13).
text.formatted: This extraction failure is not surprising, as clinical prediction models are poorly reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: For data extraction to be improved, standardised reporting guidelines for machine readable articles could be used.

We acknowledge that since our sample is based on Q1 journals, some the excess results may be due to publication bias and lower performing models were either not submitted to journals or never passed peer review (45).
text.formatted: We acknowledge that since our sample is based on Q1 journals, some the excess results may be due to publication bias and lower performing models were either not submitted to journals or never passed peer review <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(45)</ref>.

text.text: However, Q1 journals disproportionately publish prediction research and while publication bias would be a component of inflated values this is unlikely to explain the extent of inflated values at the thresholds.
Only including research from 2025 limits our results in time.
Information across years may be important to understand changes of hacking practices.
Future research examining changes in performance reporting over time could identify if these excess results at thresholds change with the growing use of AI to analyse data and write papers (46).
We found an excess of models with perfect performance values which indicates questionable practices, possibly motivated by a need to oversell model performance.
We further suspect these hacking practices are not due to alteration of in-text reporting, rather, hacking practices occur during the analysis based on our examination of ROC curves.
We expect these hacking practices primarily to come from data or methodological manipulations that inflate model performances over publication bias.
One in eight models incorrectly report the AUC value compared to the ROC curve, with some substantially and potentially clinically imported differences.

Broadly, we . identify that performance metrics in clinical prediction models are being targeted and highlight poor reporting is extensive in clinical prediction model research with more than two-thirds of articles not reporting confidence intervals and 1 in 40 AUC values with confidence intervals are errors.
Our study suggests that paper-based performance metrics may be prioritised over practical care, and this could be harming patients.
Alternatively, if none of these models made their way into practice, it may constitute an enormous volume of research waste..
